docs.dcterms_abstract: Translation [by Cristina Neagu]:  Here you can take into account two different opinions: the previous view and mine. If it were up to me to build the roof, I would make it pointed like a tower roof, and the apex would be no more than a quarter of the total length above the roofline. Additionally, if I were in charge, I would make the roof no higher than a fourth of its cross-length, and no more than two levels of beams stacked on top of each other. This would be good in terms of fire protection. I am sure, this would also be the recommendation of an authority in the field such as Vitruvius. If the old structure is too low, one could increase the height between the trusses. Add to this my view on how the long timbers should be laid and fastened on the pillars. It is, I admit, only a rough opinion, but the carpenters would know what to make of it. The hight of the roof should be about one third of its length, and it should be set on three levels of beams stacked on top of each other. The lowest level should be a quarter higher than the level above it. And the top level should be a quarter above the middle level. Thus, the structure would be error-free. The strongest wood should be used for the lowest level, the moderately strong for the middle, and the weakest wood for the top. This is how the structure should be built. It is the first and second levels that carry the roofing, and the topmost level is set as the ridge beam, resting on the two levels below. The roof should be curved inwardly on each side by a quarter, which reduces the burden. So, the entire structure should be closed in on itself. Thus it does not push against the walls, but rather supports itself. The carpenters would know what I mean. The entire roof should be laid flush onto the walls and pillars. This way it would support inself gently and naturally. It is clear that such a roof would not be affected by wind as much as a roof seven levels high would be.  It is also impossible that, if covered with thick snow, it would become as heavy as it would otherwise be. It is also more secure in terms of fire safety, if struck by lightning. And it would not cost as much in terms of day to day roof maintenance for the building. Also, the existing timberwork can be re-used, so that no great expense needs to be made for new timber. But, more importantly, I fear that, if the large roof is not removed from the church and, as a result, the building is vaulted, the roof will push the walls apart, and the structure will become damaged beyond repair.

docs.dcterms_abstract: Translation [by Cristina Neagu]:  To begin with, the question is raised whether it is more useful to leave the roof as it is or to take it down. Here follow reasons why the large roof is harmful. Firstly, it is very heavy and puts a great deal of strain on the walls. Secondly, as it is widely acknowledged, this kind of roofing pushes against the walls, which causes damage to the structure over time. Thirdly, strong winds exert force on large roofs, and this is a cause for real concern. Additionally, such a large structure is dangerous because of the risk of fire. If lightning strikes, no one would be able to save it due to the large amount of wood inside. Fifthly, maintaining such a large and unwieldy roof, taking into account all necessary repairs over time, would be much more expensive. Reasons why a smaller roof would be more practical than a large one: Firstly, such a large structure is not needed, since no grain is being stored there. Secondly, a smaller roof would not put strain on the walls, because the weight would be reduced by more than two thirds of the load. Also, the wind would blow off snow more easily. Additionally, strong winds could not exert as much force on it, since there is less resistance. A smaller structure is not as dangerous in terms of fire. If it were to burn, it would either burn faster, or it would be easier to save. Furthermore, a smaller roof would be less dangerous to build and would cost less to maintain. To conclude, a roof such as the one described above would best be one quarter of the height from its length up to the top, and would have only two trusses stacked on top of each other. This can be made from existent material, and enough timber would still be left over to build a large house from it. The roofing should be done in such a way that it holds itself together so that it does not press against the walls but instead rests upon them. Good carpenters would know what to do. If a roof with a sharp incline is still preferred, with a view to create a grain store, then two beams should be placed on each side, angled upwards by a quarter. Without the grain store, such a structure would have no purpose. But in my opinion, the best idea is to opt for a pointed roof, as described before.
